Horizon 5 is such a strange game to talk about, because while I'd say it's the best game in the series it has loads of flaws many of which have been carried forward from previous entries, sometimes over a decade old.  Mexico (and Sierra Nueva in the dlc) is an absolutely beautiful map, from the desert to the jungles to the volcano, to the mountain and the valley, to Guanajuato the extremely vibrant city. But a large portion of the map is just fields, and these fields make up the central area of the map where players are most likely to pass through. All of the amazing features of Mexico are concentrated around the outer edges of the map, and Guanajuato itself is also terribly small.   The story is bad. Awful, even. Previous entries didn't have a good story either but (aside from 4 which this is a direct sequel to) they were bad in the normal racing game way, that is to say you could just ignore it and nobody cares because we're here to race cars. Here it's just, so so so so terribly grating. Endless empty corporate positivity everywhere, the speaking of what I think was an attempt at spanglish? in a way that absolutely nobody has ever spoken. It didn't even seem out of place when I got to the hot wheels dlc and Haley just spoke advertisements for toys at me the entire time because really that's just the next logical step when your characters sit somewhere between middle management, HR personnel, and that one pepsi commercial with the riot police.  Cars are good, there's a lot of them. For the first time in the series the mods you put on can effect your engine's sound so you can audibly hear the difference between things like the exhaust options. The new handling model is rather great, though it does feel like it leads to annoying levels of oversteer on RWD cars at times. An annoying amount of cars are stuck behind wheelspins or whatever live service thing they wanted to shove in for no reason, though. Seriously you could just buy the Trueno immediately in 1-3 why have 4 and 5 decided to banish it to live service purgatory.  Unlike in 4 you can't set back the date on your computer to get old series rewards, if you're not connected to the internet it just pays out wheelspins as rewards instead. This is stupid and bad, why are you locking cars behind the auction house? There's not even a profit motive for it which makes it even stranger.  The PI system is still bad and extremely easy to game, because of the way it's calculated you can do things like have an AWD swap that costs almost nothing or cram an absurd amount of power into a given class cap because the AI driver used to calculate scores by driving it around a simulated test track always uses the default tune, so you can do things like adjust sway bars to fix understeer or adjust the gearing ratio to actually be able to use all of that power and it won't have any sort of impact on your car's class despite it clearly being much better than what the simulation suggests. This also makes online racing much less satisfying, because even without relying on these quirks to make a better build than what should be possible you can still end up with major performance discrepancies between the two PI numbers, and it can start to feel less like you're winning/losing due to skill differences and more like it's just a simple gap between the cars. Winning because I can corner better and at higher speeds is fun, winning because my car can corner better and go faster isn't.  Progression is basically nonexistent, you do races and then pick whatever story thing you wanna do next whether it's a showcase race where the rigging to be a photo finish has never been more obvious or an expedition where you drive around a closed off area of the map smashing stuff (these are still fun though). It's all entirely disconnected from me actually playing the game. There's no car class or type limitations on anything. If you wanna go through the entire game in nothing but the 2020 supra they give you at the start you can. Actually there is one limitation and that's with the midnight battles, which were added in a post-launch update and there's only 4.  Speaking of disconnected from me actually playing the game, wheelspins. Introduced in 2 (4 added junk item like horns and clothes to the pool) they're just lootboxes (you can't pay money for them though). You get either a random car, a random amount of money from 5-300k, a random piece of clothing, or a new car horn sound. Get unlucky on a wheelspin, you get basically nothing. Get lucky and suddenly you've gained either a car that sells for a substantial amount on the auction house or a bunch of credits, about 20 race's worth. At any given time I tend to be sitting on 1-3m in credits and an insignificant amount of these are actually earned via skilled racing. There's no accomplishment felt when buying one of the more expensive cars because I didn't actually *do* anything to earn it, I just got lucky on a lottery.  The livery editor and the vinyl maker are largely the same as they've been since 2. Gran Turismo has had SVG importing options since Sport which released in 2017, before Horizon 4 came out.  The AI cheats massively, if first and second can get away by the fourth corner you just restart the race because they're going to continue getting faster and faster to the point you can't catch up. Conversely if you get out in front the race is a time attack as the AI will make no attempts to overtake and will instead slowly fall further and further behind until half the pack DNFs. They have much better grip than the player and also follow the racing line extremely closely even when it's wrong, so the player can easily overtake in corners where they brake entirely too much (most noticeable on dirt or the hot wheels races)   Road, Street, and Dirt races all have mostly good layouts, and 5's new physics model makes dirt super fun to race on as well, so my only major critique here is dear god why are there so many walls. It's hard to take the McRae approach to rally when sliding slightly off the road actually means slamming in to the solid concrete wall set up right at the edge of every single corner. Also gives rise to wall riding, remove the walls and suddenly people who can't brake just go flying off the course instead of launching out of the corner in the right direction.  The anti-wall riding penalty in online is stupid. Someone slams into your rear instead of braking and you hit the wall? Five second slowdown penalty. Misjudge your braking zone and slam into the wall, stopping in the process and losing more time than taking it properly would've taken? Five second slowdown penalty. Intentionally go into a corner too fast but pull the handbrake to bounce the rear corner of your car off the wall? No penalty at all. Great system.  Cross Country races are bad. They have been bad since they were introduced in 2. I don't know who thought sweeping right into sweeping left into blind jump was good race design but it isn't. Full throttle for most of the race, and then rewind 15 times because you took the jump at a slightly wrong angle and either didn't land close enough to the checkpoint or you landed in such a way that you will go slamming into a building instead of through the narrow alley the next checkpoint is in. These are bad and they suck, please either stop making them in favor of more proper rally events or at least design them in a way that can be done without rewind.  Half the difficulty options don't even give you more credits anymore. Normal > Sim steering, Manual > M/C, Cosmetic > Full damage, and rewind off don't give more rewards despite taking more skillful play.  I really, really like the horizon series and it's a lot of fun but god does it have flaws some of which are over a decade old. Horizon 5 is still fun and it's absolutely worth the money, but it's not perfect. I really hope 6 brings major improvements to the franchise. Overall 8~9/10

This has been the first modern Forza game I've played since Forza motorsport 3 / 4 and honestly, if I could rate this as a maybe, rather than yes or no I would.   The game shoves are lot in your face from the start, and takes you out of what you're doing to show you something you probably wont care about nor want to do at that time, a notification would suffice rather than an abduction.  The map is diverse and the tracks are relatively entertaining, but dreadfully short other than for a couple specific examples that rarely come up. This is made worse by the tiny selection of them that are available to you when you go for PVP in each category, you will get to know the tracks available very quickly.  The number of manufacturers in the game is surprisingly wide, but for most the selection isn't that deep, for example the game includes a huge number of Porsche models that you will just stockpile before something interesting comes along.  Player base itself is probably one of the more ego fuelled cesspits I've come across in racing games, does not matter whether its cooperative modes or PVP, someone is out there every session to make your time miserable.  The system in place to penalise mistakes is very open to abuse, you can be rammed / T-boned / ridden into a wall and then be penalised with a speed reduction to top it off; the number of times I have been stopped dead and then suffocated by a 10 second crawl is maddening.  Rarely have I seen this trigger if you actually benefit from the contact.  This comes back to the tracks being too short, as any mistake often results in very little opportunity to catch up; you can be side by side with another player approaching a checkpoint and get pushed off the track at the last moment to miss said checkpoint, and that's it, race pretty much over for you.  With all that said, and I'm leaving things out, I probably will end up playing this with my group still, but the jury is out on whether I'll consider FH6.

This game has gone through some wild shifts and changes over the years, and it is a battle royale first and foremost above all others, so if that is not your vibe, steer clear.   That said, for a free to play adaptation from a pay to play core, PUBG has thrived since it's initial ups and downs of finding a good foothold in a market that quickly got overtaken by flashier and more cartoony competitors.    This is a great game to just casually knock out a few drops with some friends or goof off in solo que doing self imposed absurd challenges, and the casual mode doubly makes it much less of a chance of just getting completely stomped by people who eat sleep and breath the game while your just trying to play with people of varying skill level and interest in the game.   As it stands now, it is a solid free to play BR option for the people who prefer less cartoony asthetics with more realistic style firearms. It certainly is not a full hardcore vibe on the realistic feel so won't really scratch the itch there, but overall it has a lot going for it in it's specific niche.  The competitive scene is also quite impressive and for such a random variable element of a game that often comes down to luck over skill in terms of equipment strategies, it is still very entertaining to watch in spite of the inherent lack of a certain degree of mechanical balance optimization just due to the nature of the game itself.   There are also very amusing custom lobbies that can be tweaked into all kinds of improvised game modes for very silly group fun if your lucky enough to be part of a community that can muster the numbers to host such a thing!   The journey of improvement and refinement is a constant one that never truly ends however, and these are the things I think could do with some changes to improve the quality of the game and extend it's reach even further:   [b] CASUAL REWORKS [/b]   Change casual ques to 90min instead of 60min and allow groups who are queing together to go off the time remaining of the group member with the most time remaining, even if other group members have 0 time remaining themselves. people meet up and decide to do a little casual play at different points in the day, in different circles, this helps make this process not feel like a time triage excercise similar to scheduling DnD groups   [b] BOT DROP [/b]  Adding a purely co-op comp stomp mode would be very helpful for those of us who enjoy playing casuals but do not want the human competitive element in any way beyond friendly team competition to see who can get the most kills / coolest kills.   Someone like me can go toe to toe easily in the main matches and the "who's a bot and who's not" excitement of casuals is something I can handle easily enough, but for a lot of people I play with who enjoy a purely casual against bots experience that is not high pressure so they can be comfortable and spend time with friends and loved ones without getting upset or too overly stressed, something like this would be much better:   The maps are much smaller environments (they can just be zoomed in sections of already existing maps to start with, but eventually custom designed maps using pre-existing assets would be the best course of action to help with differentation at a glance and variety)   The game mode would be 100 participants, with up to 6 six slots occupied by players in one team replacing a bot spawn from either a pre-que or public lobby (with players still able to launch on less than max numbers)   Everyone parachutes in at the same time in random spots in the sky above the map and have to steer themselves into locations alongside all the bots, and then it's just a free for all as the bots do not have teams, but they always priortize engaging human players over one another (and are generally coded to miss each other as much as possible when fighting one another) they will never kill downed players intentionally, and as the match progresses and the circle tightens, the bots become universally stronger, more well equipped, and deadlier, all while ensuring their top priority is to avoid the closing circle, up to the point of not stopping to engage until they are inside of it at all costs (and also reducing outside of circle damage to the bots so a ton of them don't just die out there like in casuals)   I could elaborate a great deal on more specifics and unique elements of this game mode, but this review only has so much room so if the devs would like to contact me directly, I would happily provide additional expansion and development plans to streamline it's inception!  [b] FAT TRIMMING [/b]    There is soooo much overlapping emergency key jingling from this games years of desperate reinvention and expansion that needs cleaning up. There are so many absurd sub menus and six different currencies doing the same things that could all be solved by one that make the monetized elements far more complex and annoying to engage with.   Making a "give me all my stuff I qualify for" button that just lists a history of where and why a thing was given to the player is so much more effective and gives people a less micro management heavy way of cleanly aquiring things. It should also store and log those qualified rewards until that button IS clicked even if the event or whatever was going on has passed, so that people don't accidentally miss out on things they qualified for simply because of an arbitrary timer.   In addition, make the actual BP shop it's own thing that makes it easier to navigate what is available purely with BP without mixing it with the premium currency shop. You can still put advertisements in the BP shop items directing too premium shop versions, and you can add a premium shop currency buy options for all the BP items too even, but make the designation more clear, and simple to navigate   Again, I have a massive list of UI reconfigurations and changes to offer in great detail, along with many mechanic revisions and refinements, if the developers are interested. I understand the limitations of development especially on a skeleton crewed F2P investment anchor, but I know how to work on nothing budgets with little resources, so happy to offer my expertise if desired!   [b] NO MORE SOLO DANCES [/b]   This one is mildly irksome, but ALL dances of every kind should be group dances. This is a nitpick I will admit it, but it's just unnecissarily exclusionary in a largely team incentivizing game. Add a toggle when activating the dance for it to be solo only if you really want to keep that for more mean spirited players, but don't enforce exclusion.   I could go on an on and on about ideas for new events, tweaks and optimizations, promotional tie ins and baseline improvements but, again, due to limited space here, I'll just end on saying this game is not perfect by far, and it will be infuriating at times both because of the PVP nature of the game, and some of the games baked in elements at it's core, but if you want a slower paced BR That has less frenetic energy than other BR's and Arena Shooters while still being an engaging experience with a bit more of a "real life" influence, this one is the game for you! Black Myth Wukong is nothing short of breathtaking. From the moment you step into its myth-inspired world, the pacing hits you immediately — combat feels lightning-fast yet perfectly fluid, making every encounter a thrilling test of reflexes and precision. The game doesn’t just look cinematic, it plays cinematic, with animations that flow seamlessly even when the action gets chaotic. The music is one of the best music I have ever heard.  Black Myth Wukong is one of those rare games that instantly grabs you and doesn’t let go. I was absolutely captivated from the very beginning. What makes this title truly stand out is its unique blend of dynamic gameplay, impressive visuals, and a fresh narrative, inspired by the classic tale of Journey to the West, feels both epic and personal. It’s not just another generic fantasy plot — it brings a sense of cultural richness and mysticism that sets it apart from other action RPGs. The way the game embraces the myths and legends of ancient China gives it a flavor rarely seen in Western titles, making every encounter feel meaningful and steeped in tradition. Gameplay-wise, Black Myth: Wukong strikes a near-perfect balance between challenge and reward. The combat is fluid, fast-paced, and incredibly satisfying, with a strong emphasis on timing, strategy, and mastering different transformations and abilities. Whether you're facing a towering boss or slicing through smaller enemies, the mechanics always feel perfectly tight.  Technical side, the game is a visual powerhouse. The world design is stunning, the creature animations are top-notch, and the overall atmosphere is just breathtaking. It’s clear that an enormous amount of care has gone into every detail — from the lighting and sound design to the elaborate character, Black Myth: Wukong is a must-play. It’s a game that not only looks and plays beautifully, but also introduces something genuinely new through its cultural lens and mythical storytelling. A fresh breeze in the world of action RPGs — The Story of Monkey King Wukong is an Epic, Unforgettable Journey.  ---  9.5 / 10

Combat is pure poetry in motion. Every dodge feels earned, every strike deliberate, every boss a wall you’re meant to break — not with brute force alone, but with patience and respect. Black Myth: Wukong was an enjoyable and challenging game that, despite some optimization issues, still ran exceptionally well at times. There’s a debate about whether it should be labeled a “souls-like” game, but I personally think it fits into that category. It definitely draws inspiration from souls games, but it doesn’t compare 100%. However, it does have some similar features, such as “bonfires” boss runs and the healing gourd, which remind me of Sekiro. The game has an insane number of bosses, and while some are definitely challenging, I never found myself stuck on a boss for more than a few hours at most half a day, compared to other games in the genre. The combat is super fast-paced, and the options for different kinds of builds are cool. However, while respecing multiple times, I never found the builds really different from each other. Overall, the combat is solid and low-key addicting. For optimization issues, the game ran great for the most part. I played from chapter 1-3 on a 3060 12GB to then from chapter 3-6, I just happened to upgrade to a 5070 12GB. While the game ran great on both cards and looked really amazing on high settings, during heavy combat and character transformations, I saw insane frame drops on regular FPS and DLSS, which I had both capped at 120. It was annoying at times, especially during a boss battle, but it wasn’t a dealbreaker or anything. I see lots of reviews and articles saying the game still isn’t optimized, but for 95% of the time, it ran well. Overall, I definitely recommend this game if you are into the “souls-like genre.” My first playthrough with the “true ending” took me about 63 hours.

review_text: (Single player campaign review) This was the worst Black Ops, let alone Call of Duty game, I have played to this point.  The story of the single player campaign makes no sense, and it is not connected to the first 2 games.  The first 2 missions are used as tutorials and give you a taste of some of the tech abilities you can use within the game.  However, they leave out the names of these abilities.  Plus, they leave out where you can go to equip these abilities in the safehouse.  Example – In the second mission you get to wall run, but if you finish the mission and try to go back and wall run again – you can’t.  I had to look up online to find out where that ability could be equipped in the weapon customizations screen.  Yes, you don’t have to wall run.  You can still cross the area on a platform, but then what is the use of having that ability?  The futuristic setting with the weapons and cybertech available in the game were pretty cool, but that does not make up for how poorly this game was put together.  I’m sure the positive reviews are for the zombies, but I never really cared for those, and multiplayer is just a waste of time these days.  Now I know why Black Ops 4 does not have a single player campaign – no one at Treyarch knows how to write good stories. I would only recommend this game if you like the zombie portion of it.

game_name: Call of Duty®: Black Ops III
review_text: I launched Call of Duty on my PC for the very first time simply to see if it would run. I never completed a match, never played competitively, and never used cheats, hacks, mods, or third-party software of any kind.  Within minutes of launching the game—and without any actual gameplay—I was permanently banned at the account level.  I appealed through Activision’s official Security and Enforcement system. The appeal was denied with a generic response that cited the Terms of Use but provided no explanation, evidence, or meaningful review. I was told the decision was final.  This is not a VAC ban, yet it permanently affects my Steam profile and account features. Despite negligible playtime and no prior history, there is no transparency, no escalation path, and no consumer recourse for a paid digital product.  I support fair anti-cheat enforcement, but permanently banning accounts with minutes of activity—without explanation or proportional review—undermines trust in the system and punishes legitimate users for simply launching the game.  Buyers should be aware that you can lose access permanently with no clear reason and no meaningful way to resolve it.

game_name: Call of Duty®: Black Ops III
review_text: Zombies totally rocks in this game. It's the best zombie mode in the entire franchise by a landslide even if you don't include the incredible modding scene that the game has to this day. That alone is enough for me to recommend this game, but it's also pretty much where the praise ends.  First and most importantly: it is NOT SAFE to play any sort of public online mode in this game without a third party client. Hackers can gain a backdoor to your computer simply by being in the same lobby as you. This is an absurd vulnerability that a ton of the older CoD games have and Activision are too lazy to ever fix it.  The campaign sucks in this game. Not only is it not a continuation of any of the previous Black Ops games, but it's also narratively thin as cardboard with bad dialogue, uninteresting characters, and worse level design/gameplay than Black Ops 2 despite being 3 years newer. Also the graphics are actually pretty good for a 10 year old CoD game.  Setting aside the appalling security problems, the multiplayer is fine. Of all the futuristic CoDs, this one definitely had the maps that best accommodated the advanced movement. Otherwise, this mode really has nothing special going for it. BO3 is littered with lootboxes and DLC, and the multiplayer really suffers for it, as it is pay-to-win. If you want a good futuristic FPS, play Titanfall 2. That game is virtually perfect.  As I already said, zombies is nothing short of incredible in this game. It does an amazing job of combining the classic gameplay loop with the newer BO3 engine, and gobblegums are a fun addition (despite the monetization). Not to mention this game has a whopping 14 zombie maps! That is if you're willing to shell out a combined $80. As I said, this game is littered with DLC, and it is horrendously priced. It should honestly cost at least like half of that after all this time. Luckily, the steam workshop has literally thousands of zombie maps to pick from, many of them being on par with the kind of quality you would expect from an actual zombie map.  Overall, if money isn't tight, and you're a big fan of zombies, BO3 IS the right choice. If you're not that, there's about a thousand better Call of Duty games to pick from.

game_name: Call of Duty®: Black Ops III
review_text: The fast paced shooting of classic COD + the new abilities and movement, which was later received positively in alternate titles like Titanfall 2, works here amazingly. It mixes things up. Growing up I got tired of the history-based shooters that were common even outside of the COD series and I didn't think Halo's story and mechanics were all that good either. There was no single COD game with a campaign I cared for until this one. My first COD was 4 / Modern Warfare and I played each release up until Advanced Warfare, Black Ops 3 is the first COD campaign I played all the way until the credits. It finally felt like COD dared to be something better, or at the very least different from what it was and I was all for it.  It's got multiple zombies maps and the campaign length can vary depending on difficulty settings. Even on the easiest setting, you'll get at least 8 hours which is short compared to other genres, but tolerable when compared to $70 shooters that release with 4 hour campaigns. I highly recommend if you want a solid solo experience.   It's not something I would spend a premium on, there are other solid solo FPS games for not even half the market price of this, this is only a solid yes if you buy it on sale

review_text: I 100% recommend it for the Zombies mode, it really made this game stand the test of time and why it is still so popular over 10 years later. The custom zombies maps are exactly why I still love this game (so do many others) and even modding the base maps with weapon packs or some crazier mods still makes it a fun time. I would go as far as calling it the definitive zombies experience.  That said, the game has went the way of BO2 with hackers, cheaters and exploits resurfacing every now and then. So you need to take extra measures to ensure security even as far as avoiding the multiplayer altogether since that is the most vulnerable mode. Even though MP was fun, it was plagued by the toxic micro transaction practices of the time (this time being loot boxes) which continued into Infinite Warfare and Modern Warfare Remastered. Any DLC weapons added in via updates are locked behind weapon crates and are reliant on RNG and obscene amounts of cash being spent to obtain them. Plus COD started losing its edge/identity around this time with the cringy dance moves and victory animations contrary to popular belief it was Fortnite that caused this as COD was doing what they were doing years before.  The Campaign had some interesting ideas but was overall pretty lame and forgettable and a complete disconnect from the history and storyline established since BO1 and leading into BO2 which is why I disliked it.  It's on sale every now and then for like £15 for the game and the DLCs so wait till then, I do not recommend it for full price 10 years later.

review_text: Call of Duty: Black Ops III is one of the best entries in the franchise. The gameplay feels smooth, fast, and very responsive, making every match exciting and intense. Zombies mode is outstanding, offering deep lore, challenging maps, and great replay value, especially when playing with friends.  The campaign is unique and ambitious, with a darker tone and a story that makes you think, which sets it apart from traditional Call of Duty campaigns.  Overall, Black Ops III delivers an amazing experience with solid gameplay, great modes, and long-lasting fun. Definitely a must-play for any Call of Duty fan.

game_name: Call of Duty®: Black Ops III
review_text: Even years later, Black Ops III is still one of the strongest COD entries you can play on PC. The gameplay feels smooth and fast, with a skill gap that rewards movement, aim, and smart use of abilities. The advanced movement system adds depth without completely overwhelming new players, and it keeps matches feeling dynamic instead of repetitive.  The Zombies mode alone makes this game worth owning. With a large variety of maps, deep Easter eggs, and Steam Workshop support, BO3 offers nearly endless replayability. Custom zombies maps and mods keep the experience fresh long after the base content is finished, making it one of the best Zombies experiences in the franchise.  The campaign is darker and more experimental than most COD stories, and while it can be confusing at times, it’s ambitious and memorable if you’re willing to pay attention. Multiplayer still has a dedicated community, and when you find matches, the pacing and weapon balance feel rewarding.  Overall, BO3 is easy to recommend if you enjoy fast-paced shooters, Zombies, or modding communities. Despite its age, it holds up extremely well and offers more long-term content than many newer COD titles.
